name: Loopback network access (loopback-network)
plain: Asks to let a public site talk to services on this very computer.
meaning: Controls access to localhost services (dev servers, local agents, desktop apps). Sites used to probe localhost ports to detect installed software, so access now needs consent.

access.prompt_ui: Chrome prompt for requests from public sites to 127.0.0.1 or localhost. Legacy name local-network-access still accepted as an alias.

limits.headline: Can talk to programs on your own computer, only if you allow it in Chrome
limits.user_action: You visit a site that pairs with a desktop app and tap Allow
can: Connect to helper apps or developer tools running on this computer once you allow it
Check whether a companion app is running
Keep that access until you change it in site settings
cannot: Reach programs on your computer before you allow it
Work in Safari or on iPhone browsers
Probe your computer silently for installed apps, since the pop up blocks that
Work on Samsung Internet or Firefox the same way
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge ask with a pop up. Firefox is partial. Safari and iPhone browsers do not offer it.

story.what_it_is: Your browser asks if a website may talk to apps running on this very computer.

marketing.name: Local Network Access
marketing.pitch: Chrome now treats talking to your own computer as its own permission, separate from other devices on the network.

story.for_you: A prompt asks if the site may connect to apps on this computer. Say yes only if you installed a companion app the site works with. Otherwise block it.
story.for_makers: Makers of desktop apps with a web page front end, such as meeting, security or game launchers, use this to link the page and the app. They now need to ask and explain the benefit.

use_cases.example: A meeting site asks to connect to the desktop meeting app on your computer, so clicking Join opens the app.
A game store page asks to talk to the launcher on your PC, so Install in the browser starts the download in the app.
A password manager web page connects to its local helper, so it can fill logins in the browser.
A docs page connects to a dev server running on your laptop, to show live output.
A web music page talks to a desktop audio app, so a play button starts the local player.
A company portal checks for its endpoint security agent on this computer before login, with your permission.
A site probing your own computer for apps to build a profile is stopped by the prompt, as users see it.

technical_bounds: Exact split release version not confirmed

abuse: Port scanning to detect installed apps

history.change: Local network permission ships; later split into local-network and loopback-network
